transcript.text: I run deliveries for a grocery company in Dubai: 12 vans and about 300 orders a day, each with an address and a promised time window. Fuel and driver hours cost too much. A consultant told me to build a prediction model. I have the order log and the vans' GPS traces, but I have not exported them yet. I am the one who plans the routes every morning. Is a prediction model what I need, and what would you do first?

choices.title: Measure your baseline first
choices.what: Once you drop the two exports in this chat, I compute per-van-day numbers from the GPS traces and the order log: distance per drop, stops per hour, minutes per stop, share of deliveries landing outside the promised window, and cost per order — split by zone and by time window. You get: The honest size of the leak, and which of the three costs you money: drive time on the road, stop time at the door, or waiting (loading, parking, idling). Trade-off: It does not build tomorrow's routes. It tells you whether routing is even the problem before you spend on a model. Effort: One export of the two files; the analysis runs here.

choices.title: Build the travel-time prediction
choices.what: The useful half of the consultant's advice: a model on your GPS traces that predicts drive minutes between your zones by hour of day, including weekend and Ramadan patterns, instead of straight-line distance. You get: Realistic leg times, which is the input any route planner needs to be worth trusting in Dubai traffic. Trade-off: On its own it produces no routes — a model predicts, it does not decide. And it is worth little if the baseline shows the money leaks at the door, not on the road. Effort: Needs the GPS traces exported with timestamps; a few days of work.

choices.title: Cost brief from what you know by heart
choices.what: No export. You tell me fuel per van per day, driver wage per hour, typical stops per route, loading time at the depot, late-delivery complaints; I write a one-page brief on where the money goes and what to change this week. You get: A decision you can act on tomorrow morning — zone-based batching, tighter windows per area, fixed pickup slots, van capacity mix. Trade-off: Built on your recall, not the logs, so the numbers are soft and the saving stays an estimate. Effort: Today, in this chat.

options.tradeoff: On its own it produces no routes — a model predicts, it does not decide. And it is worth little if the baseline shows the money leaks at the door, not on the road.
options.effort: Needs the GPS traces exported with timestamps; a few days of work.

options.title: Cost brief from what you know by heart
options.what: No export. You tell me fuel per van per day, driver wage per hour, typical stops per route, loading time at the depot, late-delivery complaints; I write a one-page brief on where the money goes and what to change this week.
options.gets: A decision you can act on tomorrow morning — zone-based batching, tighter windows per area, fixed pickup slots, van capacity mix.
options.tradeoff: Built on your recall, not the logs, so the numbers are soft and the saving stays an estimate.

words:
I am an analyst at a subscription company. Please build a model that predicts churned_next_month for each customer. The table I shared has one row per customer: customer_id, signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and churned_next_month. The retention team will score all active customers at the start of each month and contact the riskiest ones. Go ahead.

(I shared a table: customers.csv)

goal.value: Train a supervised model that predicts churned_next_month (churn within the next month) for each active customer, producing a risk score per customer_id.
goal.quote: build a model that predicts churned_next_month for each customer

decision.value: Retention team ranks all active customers monthly and spends outreach capacity on the highest-risk ones; the model decides who gets contacted.
decision.quote: score all active customers at the start of each month and contact the riskiest ones

user.value: Retention team (with the analyst as the technical owner); output must be a per-customer ranking/score plus the drivers.
user.quote: The retention team will score all active customers

data.value: customers.csv, 1200 rows x 9 columns. Features: signup_date, segment, city, plan, tenure_months, monthly_spend (has missing values), support_tickets_90d. Label: churned_next_month. Leakage check on all 8 non-label columns found no column that is only known after the outcome.
data.quote: one row per customer: customer_id, signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and churned_next_month

constraints.value: Scoring happens at the start of a month, so every feature must be knowable at that moment. monthly_spend is missing for some rows and must be handled, not silently dropped.

assumptions.value: All 1200 rows describe one snapshot month (tenure_months and support_tickets_90d are measured as of that same snapshot), so the label window is the month right after the snapshot. Needs confirming.
churned_next_month = 1 means the customer cancelled within the month after the snapshot; 0 means still active.
